title: hello, goodbye, peace
hookLine: hello, goodbye, peace — and a fourth meaning: whole

cards: One word, three jobs. Someone walks in: shalom. Someone leaves: shalom.
On a card, at the end of a letter, over a door: shalom, peace. Hello, goodbye, peace. The same word opens a conversation and closes it.
But there's a fourth meaning hiding underneath the other three, and it's the one the rest of them grow from. Today, the wish folded inside the hello.

teach.b: Shalom is Hebrew, and it grows from a root of three letters, shin, lamed, mem, and the root's first sense isn't quiet. It's whole. Complete.
Nothing missing. The same root gives shalem, whole, and a verb for paying back what you owe, so the account is square again. So peace, in this language, isn't only the absence of a fight.
It's the presence of everything that should be there. A house with shalom has nothing broken in it. A body with shalom is well.

teach.h: SEE THE SHALOM OF YOUR BROTHERS.
teach.b: In the Torah, when Jacob sends his son Joseph to check on his brothers, the Hebrew says, more or less: go and see the shalom of your brothers. How whole are they? The word runs all through Jewish prayer.
The priestly blessing, said over congregations, and in some homes over the children on Friday night, ends with it: "and give thee peace." Peace is the last word.

And an old psalm doesn't treat peace as something that just happens to you: "Seek peace, and pursue it." The rabbis noticed that verb. Other commandments, they taught, you do when the chance comes to you.
Peace you go after. So when someone says shalom at a door, coming or going, underneath the hello is an old wish: may you be whole.

how: Shalom is said as hello and goodbye, and Shabbat shalom on the Sabbath; the priestly blessing, which ends with a prayer for peace, is said in synagogue and in some homes by parents over their children on Friday night.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: its root means whole: the presence of everything that should be there.
the priestly blessing ends with the word for peace
"and give thee peace": shalom is its last word.
the Psalms say to wait for peace to arrive
"seek peace, and pursue it." the rabbis noticed: peace is chased.

games.q: Jacob sends Joseph to check on his brothers in the fields. in the Hebrew, what does he tell him to go and see?
games.why: go and see the shalom of your brothers: how whole they are. the Bible asks how someone is by asking after their shalom.

practice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Breathe slowly, and notice one place in you that feels not quite whole right now. Tired.
Worried. Rushed. Don't fix it; just let it be noticed.
On the last breath, if you want to, say the word, out loud or inside: shalom. Not to fix anything. Just to wish it whole.

wordCard.voice: Shalom. Hello, goodbye, peace, and underneath all three: whole, with nothing missing. Twelfth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: from the root sh-l-m, whole or complete.

carryVoice: Your line: be whole. It's the wish folded inside every hello and goodbye. That's day twelve.

sources.ref: Leviticus Rabbah 9:9 (other commandments when the chance comes; peace is pursued)
